analysis.one_liner: Sends $2,000 per month to every American for the length of the coronavirus crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have paid each adult $2,000 a month for up to 12 months, never got a hearing or a vote in the House Ways and Means Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, this bill would have directed the Treasury to send $2,000 per month to every adult ($4,000 per married couple), plus $500 per child ($1,500 for three or more children), for a 12-month period that could end early only if employment recovered strongly. Payments would phase out for individuals making over $130,000 (over $260,000 for couples), would not count as income for taxes or for benefit eligibility, and would reach people without fixed addresses and non-citizens who had been continuously in the U.S. since late January 2020. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, most adults in the country — including people without bank accounts or fixed addresses, people whose only income comes from VA or Social Security checks, and non-citizens continuously present in the U.S. since January 27, 2020 — would have received $2,000 a month for up to a year, with extra for each child. Payments would not have counted against eligibility for other federal or state benefits, so no one would have lost aid for accepting the money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Adults and teens 16 and older, especially low- and middle-income households

how_it_helps.text: Provides $2,000 per month ($4,000 for joint filers) to each eligible individual for a 12-month payment period, starting within 14 days of enactment.
Adds $500 per dependent child, rising to $1,500 for families with three or more children.
Extends the payment period beyond 12 months unless the employment-to-population ratio for people 16 and over rises above 60 percent, tying the payments to actual job-market recovery.

Requires the Treasury to pay people without fixed addresses and to offer payment by direct deposit, check, prepaid debit card, or a mobile electronic transfer application, so people without bank accounts could receive the money.

Makes payments tax-free and disregards them as income or resources for 12 months when determining eligibility for any federal, state, or federally funded local benefits, so recipients would not lose other aid.
Requires Treasury to use VA and Social Security records for people without sufficient tax return information and to set up an application process and a 24-hour toll-free hotline for everyone else.

Extends eligibility to non-citizens who are not U.S. residents but were physically present in the United States continuously since January 27, 2020, the date the COVID-19 public health emergency took effect.

analysis.who_pays: The bill appropriates whatever sums are necessary directly from the Treasury, with no tax increase or spending offset attached. The cost of sending roughly $2,000 a month to the large majority of adults for a year would run to trillions of dollars of federal spending, financed by borrowing, with the burden ultimately falling on federal taxpayers generally. Individuals earning over $130,000 and couples over $260,000 receive nothing as their income rises past those thresholds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, through trillions in new borrowing

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as may be necessary' with no revenue source or offset, so the entire cost would be added to the federal deficit.

The phaseout is steep only above very high incomes: a couple earning just under $260,000 would still have received $48,000 over the year, and the $500-per-child bump applies regardless of family income below the threshold.

Including non-citizens who are not U.S. residents but have been continuously present since January 27, 2020, was certain to be a point of sharp political opposition, and the bill offered no compromise language on it.

The automatic extension trigger (employment-to-population above 60 percent) ties federal payments to a single statistic that shifts for reasons unrelated to the pandemic, making the program's end date hard to predict.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing pandemic job loss, $24,000 per adult over a year would have far exceeded the one-time $1,200 checks in the spring 2020 relief law. But the bill's design invited legitimate objections: it placed no dollar ceiling on the total cost, left the deficit to absorb everything, and set payment cutoffs so high that substantial sums would have flowed to upper-middle-income households. A more targeted or offset version might have cleared the political bar; this one never got that hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2021 with no vote ever held.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Ryan introduced the bill on April 14, 2020, during the first months of the COVID-19 emergency, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Forty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.
The action history shows no further steps after the referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill expired without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above the bill's $130,000/$260,000 income cutoffs were spared a large share of the trillions in costs, and no offsetting taxes were ever enacted. American workers did not receive the payments the bill promised, and the assistance that did pass that spring took other forms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-income households spared the cost; workers got nothing

for.name: Tim Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Money for the People Act and recruited 42 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 42 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, lending it enough Democratic support to appear on the radar but far short of what a floor vote requires.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or committee vote; the committee took no action on it after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats and no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the bill's support never extended beyond one party; no Republican acted on it either way.

industries.note: These households would have received sharply reduced or no payments while sharing the general tax burden of a multi-trillion-dollar program. Their gain from the bill dying is the public's loss in this frame, since the money not spent would otherwise have gone to working households.
Every adult would have received cash, but the bill's open-ended appropriation means the same population would bear the cost of servicing trillions in new federal borrowing over time.
